Where it began

Yograj Singh's roots are in Kanech, a village close to Doraha in the Ludhiana district of Punjab. He bowled right-arm fast-medium, and the first sign of what he could do came in 1977, when India's Under-22 side picked him to play England at Nagpur.

Two years later he lined up for the Board President's XI against the touring Pakistanis at Baroda. He took three for 29 there, and two of the wickets were big ones: Javed Miandad and Wasim Raja. The selectors took notice.

The player

In 1980 he was chosen for India's tour of Australia and New Zealand. His first one-day international came against New Zealand at Brisbane on 21 December 1980, and he took two for 44 from 8.4 overs. He went on to play six one-day internationals in all.

His Test debut followed at Wellington on 21 February 1981. He bowled only in the first innings and took one wicket, and a good one: John Wright. New Zealand won the match by 62 runs. It turned out to be his only Test, with one wicket for 63 and 10 runs from his two innings. An injury cut short his playing career.

What made him special

Yograj was a lively seamer, good enough to be picked by India in both forms of the game and to dismiss Javed Miandad on his way there. Batting was more of a side interest. His top score in Tests was 6, and nobody ever accused him of hogging the strike.

His son Yuvraj Singh went on to play for India from 2000 to 2017, so the family name was on Indian teamsheets for a good many years.

A second career on screen

When his cricket ended, Yograj turned to films. He made his acting debut in the Punjabi film Batwara in 1983, and through the 1980s and 1990s he became one of the leading stars of Punjabi cinema, often as the main villain opposite Gugu Gill. He worked behind the camera too. He wrote and directed Vichhora in 1994, and also directed or produced Jatt Punjab Da in 1992 and Love U Bobby in 2009.

Hindi film audiences came to know him through Teen Thay Bhai, the British-Indian film West is West (2010) and the comedy Singh Is Bliing (2015). His best-known role was the strict athletics coach Havildar Sampuran Singh in Bhaag Milkha Bhaag (2013), which brought him recognition right across India. He kept working in Punjabi films as well, appearing in Sajjan Singh Rangroot in 2018 and Ardaas Karaan a year later.

And finally

One Test, one wicket and a list of films long enough to need its own page. Few cricketers find their most famous role more than thirty years after their Test debut. Fewer again do it by playing a coach so well that it made his name across India.
